definition.text: The extra revenue a firm earns by selling one more unit of its product.

facts.text: In a perfectly competitive market a firm gets the same price for every unit, so its marginal revenue equals the price.
A monopoly must cut its price on all units to sell one more, so its marginal revenue is always below the price.
Example: selling 20 books at $50 brings $1000, and 21 books at $49 brings $1029, so the 21st book adds $29.
A firm maximises profit where marginal revenue equals marginal cost; it is making money on extra units while marginal revenue is higher.
When demand is inelastic, selling more forces a price cut on every unit and marginal revenue turns negative.
Under perfect competition the marginal revenue curve is a flat line at the market price; for a monopoly it slopes down and lies below the demand curve.

definition.text: A measure of market power: the gap between price and marginal cost as a share of price, named after economist Abba Lerner.

facts.text: At the profit-maximising point, (P − MC)/P equals minus one over the elasticity of demand, so less elastic demand means a higher markup.
It runs from zero in a perfectly competitive market to 1; the closer to 1, the bigger the gap between price and marginal cost.

title: Market clearing

definition.text: The process by which a market's price settles where the amount supplied equals the amount demanded, leaving neither a surplus nor a shortage.

facts.text: The market-clearing price, also called the equilibrium price, is the one at which quantity supplied equals quantity demanded.
A price above it builds up unsold stock; a price below it leaves buyers short, sometimes unable to find the product at any price.
After an earthquake destroys homes, a housing shortage pushes prices up, builders build more, and supply rises until it meets the new demand.
Shops discount leftover Christmas decorations after Christmas until shoppers buy the excess supply.
From about 1785 to 1935 most economists took market clearing for granted, until the Great Depression's long mass unemployment led Keynes and others to doubt it.
Most economists now see continuous market clearing as unrealistic but useful for long-run analysis.

contested_note: Since the Great Depression economists have disagreed over whether prices adjust quickly enough for markets to clear, with some blaming sticky prices and others blaming unions or government policy.

definition.text: An economic system in which decisions about investment, production and distribution are guided by prices set through supply and demand.

facts.text: Market economies range from barely regulated free-market systems to interventionist ones where governments correct market failures and promote welfare.
They need clearly defined, enforceable property rights, though these need not be private: co-operatives and state firms can also trade in markets.
A price system signals people to adjust what they produce and invest; strong demand with limited supply pushes prices up and invites more production.
Governments can set price ceilings or floors, such as minimum wages, or use Pigovian taxes to deal with externalities.
Joseph Stiglitz argues markets suffer from imperfect information and need government action to fix widespread market failures.
A sustainable market economy tries to balance growth with environmental protection, using tax incentives, carbon trading and environmental rules.
